abstract.para: In modern Linux environments running KVM, hardware-assisted virtualization forms the foundation for running &vmguest;s. KVM leverages CPU extensions such as Intel VT-x or AMD-V—to execute &vmguest; operating systems safely and efficiently on the &vmhost;.
Depending on the guest operating system and its driver stack, virtual machines under KVM operate using two primary approaches, full virtualization and PVHVM/Virtio.

listitem.para: In full virtualization mode (Hardware Virtual Machine / HVM), the hypervisor presents a fully virtualized, standard hardware environment to the &vmguest;. Unmodified operating systems (such as Windows, legacy Linux, or proprietary OSs) can run without any internal modifications. By default, physical devices (legacy NICs, IDE controllers, graphics) are emulated in software via QEMU, ensuring broad compatibility at the cost of higher CPU overhead for I/O operations.

varlistentry.term: Paravirtualized Drivers and Hypervisor Enlightenments (PVHVM / Virtio)

listitem.para: Rather than relying on full software emulation for I/O operations, modern virtual machines use the industry-standard virtio paravirtualized (PV) drivers and hypervisor enlightenments. Virtio drivers allow the &vmguest; to communicate directly with the &vmhost; for block storage, networking, memory ballooning, and serial communication, bypassing slow legacy device emulation. Features such as Hyper-V enlightenments for Windows guests or Linux-native paravirtualized clock and interrupt handling significantly reduce hypervisor context switches and timer overhead.

tip.para: Modern Linux distributions such as &productname; include virtio drivers out of the box. For guest operating systems that do not ship with built-in virtio drivers (such as Windows Server), SUSE provides the SUSE Virtual Machine Drivers Pack (VMDP).
